Simplicial complexes: the shape of an interaction space

honets

2026-08-26

Each section below is one verb, worked end to end on the same data. The sections run in order in a single R session, so later ones may reuse objects the earlier ones built.

build_simplicial(): from a network to a shape

The analytic question

A graph records which pairs of things are related. A simplicial complex records which groups are related — and, crucially, it is closed under subsets: if {A, B, C} is a relation, so are {A, B}, {A, C} and {B, C}.

That closure is not bookkeeping. It is what gives the object a geometry, and therefore a topology: connected pieces, loops, voids. Those are properties no pairwise summary can express.

build_simplicial() builds one three ways, selected with type =.

library(honets)
set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(runif(100), 10, 10)
m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
diag(m) <- 0
dimnames(m) <- list(LETTERS[1:10], LETTERS[1:10])

type = "clique" — from a network

Every clique in the thresholded graph becomes a simplex. A triangle of mutually-connected nodes becomes a filled 2-simplex.

sc <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = 0.5)
sc
Clique Complex 
  10 nodes, 51 simplices, dimension 3
  Density: 13.2%  |  Mean dim: 1.18  |  Euler: -1
  f-vector: (f0=10 f1=24 f2=15 f3=2)
  Betti: b0=1 b1=2
  Nodes: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J

Ten nodes carry 51 simplices up to dimension 3: 24 edges, 15 triangles and 2 tetrahedra.

as.data.frame(sc, top = 5)
  id dim size members
1  1   0    1       E
2  2   0    1       G
3  3   0    1       F
4  4   0    1       I
5  5   1    2    E, I
as.data.frame(sc, what = "f_vector")
  dim count
1   0    10
2   1    24
3   2    15
4   3     2

The f-vector counts faces by dimension and is the complex’s basic fingerprint. dim = 0 are vertices, 1 edges, 2 triangles, 3 tetrahedra.

as.data.frame(sc, dim = 3, top = 3)
  id dim size    members
1 25   3    4 A, D, E, I
2 38   3    4 A, C, E, I

Seeing the complex

plot() draws the face counts by dimension and the complex itself.

plot(sc)

threshold decides the shape

This is the consequential parameter, and its effect is not monotone in any simple way.

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7), function(t) {
  s <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = t)
  fv <- as.data.frame(s, what = "f_vector")
  b <- betti_numbers(s)
  e <- euler_characteristic(s)
  data.frame(threshold = t, simplices = sum(fv$count), dimension = max(fv$dim),
             euler = e,
             b0 = b[["b0"]], b1 = b[["b1"]])
}))
  threshold simplices dimension euler b0 b1
1       0.3       299         6     1  1  0
2       0.4       174         5     2  1  0
3       0.5        51         3    -1  1  2
4       0.6        31         2    -3  1  4
5       0.7        18         1     2  2  0

Watch b1, the number of one-dimensional holes. It is 0 at threshold 0.3, rises to 4 at 0.6, then collapses to 0 at 0.7. At a low threshold the graph is dense enough that every loop is filled in; at a high one it is too sparse to form loops at all. The interesting structure lives in between.

That instability is the whole argument for persistent_homology(), which sweeps the threshold instead of committing to one. Never report a Betti number from a single arbitrary threshold without showing the sweep.

type = "vr" — from a distance matrix

The Vietoris-Rips complex connects points closer than a scale, then fills in every resulting clique. It is the standard construction for point-cloud data.

set.seed(2)
pts <- matrix(rnorm(40), 20, 2)
d <- as.matrix(dist(pts))
sv <- build_simplicial(d, type = "vr", threshold = 1.5, max_dim = 3L)
sv
Vietoris-Rips Complex 
  20 nodes, 6195 simplices, dimension 3
  Density: 100.0%  |  Mean dim: 2.74  |  Euler: -3875
  f-vector: (f0=20 f1=190 f2=1140 f3=4845)
  Betti: b0=1 b3=3876

max_dim is not optional here

A VR complex grows combinatorially. On this 20-point cloud:

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(2L, 3L, 4L), function(md) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  s <- build_simplicial(d, type = "vr", threshold = 1.5, max_dim = md)
  fv <- as.data.frame(s, what = "f_vector")
  data.frame(max_dim = md, simplices = sum(fv$count),
             seconds = round(proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0, 2))
}))
  max_dim simplices seconds
1       2      1350    0.07
2       3      6195    0.20
3       4     21699    0.88

Roughly a 3-4× increase per dimension. At the default max_dim = 10L this same 20-point cloud produces 784,625 simplices and takes minutes — so for VR complexes, set max_dim deliberately. Dimensions above 3 rarely carry interpretable structure, and persistent_homology() defaults to max_dim = 3L for exactly this reason.

type = "pathway" — from a memory network

The third route takes a fitted model from the memory family and turns its extracted paths into simplices. See pathways() for what each model contributes.

seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
hon <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 2, min_freq = 50)
build_simplicial(hon, type = "pathway")
Pathway Complex 
  9 nodes, 29 simplices, dimension 2
  Density: 22.5%  |  Mean dim: 0.90  |  Euler: 1
  f-vector: (f0=9 f1=14 f2=6)
  Betti: b0=2 b1=1
  Nodes: Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify

Here b0 = 2 says the well-evidenced pathways split into two disconnected groups of actions — a statement about the corpus that the transition network cannot make.

Checking the construction

verify_simplicial() re-derives the f-vector independently, as a guard against a mis-specified threshold or a malformed matrix.

verify_simplicial(m, threshold = 0.5)
  Cliques:  MATCH (51 simplices)
  Betti:    b0=1 b1=2 b2=0 b3=0
  Euler:    -1 (Euler-Poincare: VERIFIED)

It also confirms the Euler-Poincaré identity — the alternating sum of the f-vector equals the alternating sum of the Betti numbers:

fv <- as.data.frame(sc, what = "f_vector")
sum(fv$count * (-1)^fv$dim)
[1] -1
euler_characteristic(sc)
[1] -1

Both give −1. If they ever disagree, the homology computation is wrong.

What to do next

  • betti_numbers() — what the holes mean, and how to read them.
  • persistent_homology() — the answer to the threshold problem above.
  • q_analysis() — connectivity at each level of overlap, and per-node higher-order degree.
  • build_hypergraph() — the same cliques without the subset-closure requirement.

References

  • Edelsbrunner, H., & Harer, J. (2010). Computational Topology: An Introduction. American Mathematical Society.
  • Zomorodian, A., & Carlsson, G. (2005). Computing persistent homology. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 33(2), 249-274.

betti_numbers(): counting holes

The analytic question

Once a set of relations has been made into a simplicial complex, it has a shape — and a shape can be counted. Betti numbers count the holes, one number per dimension:

  • b0 — connected components. How many separate pieces?
  • b1 — one-dimensional holes. Loops that are not filled in.
  • b2 — two-dimensional voids. Cavities enclosed by triangles.

The useful ones are b1 and b2, because they detect absence. A loop in b1 is a cycle of relations where every consecutive pair is present but the interior is not — a near-miss. Frequency-based summaries cannot see those; they only report what happened.

library(honets)
set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(runif(100), 10, 10)
m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
diag(m) <- 0
dimnames(m) <- list(LETTERS[1:10], LETTERS[1:10])
sc <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = 0.5)

Counting

betti_numbers(sc)
b0 b1 b2 b3 
 1  2  0  0

One connected component, two independent loops, no voids. The two loops are the finding: pairs of nodes are connected all the way round a cycle, but the cycle is never completed into filled triangles.

The Euler characteristic

euler_characteristic() compresses the whole shape into one integer — the alternating sum of face counts.

euler_characteristic(sc)
[1] -1

It can be computed two entirely different ways, and they must agree. That is the Euler-Poincaré identity, and it is the best available check that the homology computation is correct.

fv <- as.data.frame(sc, what = "f_vector")
fv
  dim count
1   0    10
2   1    24
3   2    15
4   3     2
# from the faces: f0 - f1 + f2 - f3
sum(fv$count * (-1)^fv$dim)
[1] -1
# from the holes: b0 - b1 + b2 - b3
b <- betti_numbers(sc)
sum(b * (-1)^(seq_along(b) - 1))
[1] -1

All three give −1. If they diverge, something is wrong — this identity is worth asserting in any pipeline that computes homology.

Betti numbers are threshold-dependent

This is the caveat that matters most.

do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0.3, 0.75, by = 0.05), function(t) {
  s <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = t)
  fv <- as.data.frame(s, what = "f_vector")
  b <- betti_numbers(s)
  e <- euler_characteristic(s)
  data.frame(threshold = t, simplices = sum(fv$count),
             b0 = b[["b0"]], b1 = b[["b1"]],
             euler = e)
}))
   threshold simplices b0 b1 euler
1       0.30       299  1  0     1
2       0.35       229  1  0     1
3       0.40       174  1  0     2
4       0.45        75  1  0     5
5       0.50        51  1  2    -1
6       0.55        34  1  3    -2
7       0.60        31  1  4    -3
8       0.65        26  1  3    -2
9       0.70        18  2  0     2
10      0.75        14  6  0     6

b1 is 0, then 2, then 4, then 0 across a modest range of thresholds. A paper reporting “the complex has two loops” without the threshold is reporting an artefact of an arbitrary choice.

Two honest ways to handle it:

  1. Show the sweep, as above, and describe how the count behaves.
  2. Use persistent_homology(), which sweeps the threshold automatically and reports how long each feature survives. A loop that persists across many scales is real; one that appears at a single threshold is noise.

Seeing the sweep

The table above is a curve. Plotting it is the honest way to report a threshold-dependent invariant: it shows the whole range rather than the one threshold that happened to be chosen.

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0.3, 0.75, by = 0.05), function(t) {
  s <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = t)
  b <- betti_numbers(s)
  data.frame(threshold = t, dimension = c("b0", "b1"),
             betti = c(b[["b0"]], b[["b1"]]))
}))
ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(x = threshold, y = betti,
                                   colour = dimension, shape = dimension)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(b0 = "#0072B2", b1 = "#D55E00")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "threshold", y = "Betti number", colour = NULL,
                shape = NULL,
                title = "Betti numbers across the threshold sweep") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

On real data

seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
hon <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 3, min_freq = 5)
sc_hon <- build_simplicial(hon, type = "pathway")
sc_hon
Pathway Complex 
  9 nodes, 157 simplices, dimension 3
  Density: 61.6%  |  Mean dim: 1.87  |  Euler: 19
  f-vector: (f0=9 f1=36 f2=79 f3=33)
  Betti: b0=1 b2=18
  Nodes: Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify 
betti_numbers(sc_hon)
b0 b1 b2 b3 
 1  0 18  0

b0 = 1: the pathway complex is connected — no group of actions is isolated. b1 = 0: every loop of actions is filled in by some observed pathway. b2 = 18: there are 18 independent two-dimensional voids — configurations of four actions where every triple was observed but the four-way combination never was.

Those 18 are the corpus’s near-misses: patterns the sessions came right up to the edge of and never completed. That is a claim about what is absent, which is why it needed a topological method to find.

What to do next

  • persistent_homology() — the threshold problem, solved properly.
  • q_analysis() — a different notion of connectivity: how strongly do the groups overlap?
  • build_simplicial() — the constructions these numbers describe.

References

  • Edelsbrunner, H., & Harer, J. (2010). Computational Topology: An Introduction. American Mathematical Society.
  • Ghrist, R. (2008). Barcodes: The persistent topology of data. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 45(1), 61-75.

persistent_homology(): which features are real

The analytic question

betti_numbers() counts holes at one threshold, and the count is unstable: change the threshold slightly and loops appear and vanish. Any single-threshold result is partly an artefact of the choice.

persistent_homology() removes the choice. It sweeps the threshold across the whole range, tracks every feature from the scale where it is born to the scale where it dies, and reports how long each survived. Features that persist across many scales are structural; features that flicker in and out at one scale are noise.

This turns “how many holes?” — which has no threshold-free answer — into “which holes are robust?”, which does.

library(honets)
set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(runif(100), 10, 10)
m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
diag(m) <- 0
dimnames(m) <- list(LETTERS[1:10], LETTERS[1:10])

Running it

ph <- persistent_homology(m, n_steps = 12, max_dim = 2)
ph
Persistent Homology
  12 filtration steps [0.9288 → 0.0093]
  Features: b0: 9 (1 persistent)  |  b1: 4 (0 persistent)  |  b2: 84 (84 persistent) 
  Longest-lived:
    b0: 0.9288 → 0.0000 (life: 0.9288)
    b2: 0.5113 → 0.0000 (life: 0.5113)
    b2: 0.5113 → 0.0000 (life: 0.5113)

The persistence diagram

One row per feature: the dimension it lives in, where it was born, where it died, and the difference.

as.data.frame(ph, sort_by = "persistence", top = 8)
  dimension     birth death persistence
1         0 0.9287756     0   0.9287756
2         2 0.5113141     0   0.5113141
3         2 0.5113141     0   0.5113141
4         2 0.4918348     0   0.4918348
5         2 0.4770873     0   0.4770873
6         2 0.4770873     0   0.4770873
7         2 0.4767907     0   0.4767907
8         2 0.4767907     0   0.4767907

persistence is the column that matters. The top feature — a 0-dimensional class with persistence 0.93 — is the connected component that survives the entire filtration. Everything below it is short-lived by comparison.

Note that birth exceeds death here. The filtration runs from a high weight threshold down to a low one, so features are born at high weights and die as the complex fills in. Persistence is the length of the interval either way.

Reading one dimension at a time

as.data.frame(ph, dimension = 1, sort_by = "persistence", top = 5)
  dimension     birth     death persistence
1         1 0.6902048 0.4918348   0.1983700
2         1 0.6880047 0.4999354   0.1880693
3         1 0.6853510 0.5633173   0.1220338
4         1 0.6348426 0.5245315   0.1103111
as.data.frame(ph, dimension = 0, sort_by = "persistence", top = 5)
  dimension     birth     death persistence
1         0 0.9287756 0.0000000   0.9287756
2         0 0.9287756 0.6951440   0.2336316
3         0 0.9287756 0.7054163   0.2233593
4         0 0.9287756 0.7084508   0.2203248
5         0 0.9287756 0.7358231   0.1929525

Dimension 0 is the merge history of connected components — each row is two pieces joining. Dimension 1 is loops, dimension 2 voids.

Betti curves

The same information viewed as counts against threshold, rather than as intervals.

as.data.frame(ph, what = "betti", top = 8)
  threshold dimension betti
1 0.9287756         0     9
2 0.8451858         0     8
3 0.7615960         0     7
4 0.6780062         0     1
5 0.5944164         0     1
6 0.5108266         0     1
7 0.4272368         0     1
8 0.3436470         0     1

Read the b0 column down: 9 components at the highest threshold, then 8, 7, and then 1 — the graph rapidly coalesces into a single piece as the threshold falls. That transition point is where the network “connects”, and it is visible here without having to pick a threshold in advance.

Plotting

if (requireNamespace("gridExtra", quietly = TRUE)) plot(ph)

The diagram plots death against birth; points far from the diagonal are the persistent features. The Betti curves show the counts across the sweep.

Choosing n_steps and max_dim

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(6L, 12L, 24L), function(ns) {
  p <- persistent_homology(m, n_steps = ns, max_dim = 2)
  d <- as.data.frame(p)
  data.frame(n_steps = ns, features = nrow(d),
             max_persistence = round(max(d$persistence), 4))
}))
  n_steps features max_persistence
1       6       97          0.9288
2      12       97          0.9288
3      24       97          0.9288

n_steps controls the resolution of the sweep — more steps locate births and deaths more precisely, at linear cost. The longest-lived feature is stable across resolutions, which is the reassurance you want: the headline finding does not depend on the grid.

max_dim is the expensive one. It defaults to 3L here (rather than the 10L that build_simplicial() uses) precisely because complexes grow combinatorially with dimension. Raise it only if you have a reason to expect structure above dimension 3.

Essential classes

d <- as.data.frame(ph)
sum(!is.finite(d$death))
[1] 0

Features that never die are reported with death = Inf. There are none in this filtration because it runs to completion. When comparing diagrams with bottleneck_distance(), essential classes need explicit handling — the reference implementations differ on whether to include them.

Validation

The Z/2 boundary-matrix reduction behind this verb is checked against ripser (via TDAstats) in the package’s equivalence suite: 30 random point clouds, maximum discrepancy 4.44e-16 — machine precision.

What to do next

  • persistence_landscape() — turn a diagram into something you can average, plot and compare statistically.
  • betti_numbers() — the single-threshold version, and why it needs a sweep.
  • build_simplicial() — the complexes this filters over.

References

  • Edelsbrunner, H., Letscher, D., & Zomorodian, A. (2002). Topological persistence and simplification. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 28, 511-533.
  • Zomorodian, A., & Carlsson, G. (2005). Computing persistent homology. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 33(2), 249-274.
  • Ghrist, R. (2008). Barcodes: The persistent topology of data. Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society, 45(1), 61-75.

Comparing persistence diagrams

The analytic question

A persistence diagram is a multiset of points — not a vector, not a function. You cannot average two of them, feed one to a regression, or compute a standard deviation across a sample. That is inconvenient the moment you want to compare two datasets rather than describe one.

Two verbs solve it in different ways:

  • bottleneck_distance() gives a metric: how far apart are these two diagrams? Good for a direct comparison, and it is the classical stability distance for persistence.
  • persistence_landscape() gives a function: it re-encodes the diagram as a sequence of piecewise-linear functions living in a vector space, where averaging and statistics are ordinary operations.
library(honets)
mk <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  m <- matrix(runif(100), 10, 10)
  m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
  diag(m) <- 0
  dimnames(m) <- list(LETTERS[1:10], LETTERS[1:10])
  persistent_homology(m, n_steps = 12, max_dim = 2)
}
ph  <- mk(1)
ph2 <- mk(9)

Bottleneck distance

bottleneck_distance(ph, ph2)
     dim_0      dim_1      dim_2 
0.10570661 0.09403464 0.12921179

One value per dimension: components, loops, voids. These two random networks differ most in dimension 2 (0.129) and least in dimension 1 (0.094).

Restrict to a single dimension with dimension =:

bottleneck_distance(ph, ph2, dimension = 1)
     dim_1 
0.09403464

It is a metric, and you should check that

# identity of indiscernibles: d(x, x) = 0
bottleneck_distance(ph, ph)
dim_0 dim_1 dim_2 
    0     0     0 
# symmetry: d(x, y) = d(y, x)
d_12 <- bottleneck_distance(ph, ph2)
d_21 <- bottleneck_distance(ph2, ph)
identical(d_12, d_21)
[1] TRUE

Both hold exactly. The bottleneck distance is the smallest ε such that the two diagrams can be matched within ε, allowing unmatched points to pair with the diagonal — which is what makes it robust to the short-lived noise features that clutter every diagram.

Persistence landscapes

A landscape converts the diagram into k_max functions. The first, k = 1, traces the most persistent feature at each scale; k = 2 the second-most, and so on.

pl <- persistence_landscape(ph, k_max = 3, dimension = 1)
pl
Persistence Landscape (dimension 1, k_max = 3)
  Evaluated at 200 grid points in [0.4918, 0.6902]
  Sup norms by k: k1=0.0987  k2=0.0936  k3=0.0609

The sup norms summarise each level in one number: k1 = 0.0987, k2 = 0.0936, k3 = 0.0609. The first two are close, meaning this filtration has two comparably prominent loops rather than one dominant one — consistent with b1 = 2 from betti_numbers().

as.data.frame(pl, top = 4)
  k         t        value
1 1 0.4918348 0.0000000000
2 1 0.4928316 0.0009968344
3 1 0.4938284 0.0019936688
4 1 0.4948253 0.0029905032

One row per (level, grid point). Restrict to one level with k =:

as.data.frame(pl, k = 1, top = 3)
  k         t        value
1 1 0.4918348 0.0000000000
2 1 0.4928316 0.0009968344
3 1 0.4938284 0.0019936688
pl_1 <- as.data.frame(pl, k = 1)
nrow(pl_1)
[1] 200

200 grid points per level, which is t_grid’s default resolution.

Plotting

plot(pl)

Why a landscape rather than a diagram

Because it lives in a vector space, a landscape supports operations a diagram does not:

land_1 <- persistence_landscape(ph,  k_max = 2, dimension = 1)
land_2 <- persistence_landscape(ph2, k_max = 2, dimension = 1)
l1 <- as.data.frame(land_1, k = 1)
l2 <- as.data.frame(land_2, k = 1)

# the two landscapes are evaluated on different grids by default
range(l1$t)
[1] 0.4918348 0.6902048
range(l2$t)
[1] 0.4520990 0.6070456

Note the grids differ — each landscape is evaluated over its own diagram’s range. To average or subtract landscapes, put them on a common grid with t_grid:

g <- seq(0.45, 0.75, length.out = 100)
land_a <- persistence_landscape(ph,  k_max = 2, dimension = 1, t_grid = g)
land_b <- persistence_landscape(ph2, k_max = 2, dimension = 1, t_grid = g)
a <- as.data.frame(land_a, k = 1)
b <- as.data.frame(land_b, k = 1)

mean_landscape <- data.frame(t = g, value = (a$value + b$value) / 2)

# L2 distance between the two, on the shared grid
sqrt(sum((a$value - b$value)^2) * diff(g)[1])
[1] 0.02211789

A mean landscape is a landscape, so it plots like one:

both <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = g, value = a$value,           landscape = "A"),
  data.frame(t = g, value = b$value,           landscape = "B"),
  data.frame(t = g, value = mean_landscape$value, landscape = "mean")
)
ggplot2::ggplot(both, ggplot2::aes(x = t, y = value,
                                   colour = landscape, linetype = landscape)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(A = "#0072B2", B = "#D55E00", mean = "#009E73")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "filtration parameter t", y = expression(lambda^(1)),
                colour = NULL, linetype = NULL,
                title = "Two landscapes and their pointwise mean") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

That mean is a legitimate object — the average of two persistence landscapes is itself a persistence landscape. The average of two persistence diagrams is not well defined at all. This is the entire reason landscapes exist.

Choosing between them

  • bottleneck_distance() — comparing two datasets, or checking stability under perturbation. Returns one interpretable number per dimension. Slower on large diagrams, since it solves a matching problem.
  • persistence_landscape() — many datasets, or any analysis needing means, variances or a regression. Fix t_grid across the sample, or the results are not comparable.

What to do next

  • persistent_homology() — where the diagrams come from.
  • betti_numbers() — the single-threshold summary these methods generalise.

References

  • Bubenik, P. (2015). Statistical topological data analysis using persistence landscapes. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 16, 77-102.
  • Cohen-Steiner, D., Edelsbrunner, H., & Harer, J. (2007). Stability of persistence diagrams. Discrete & Computational Geometry, 37(1), 103-120.
  • Kerber, M., Morozov, D., & Nigmetov, A. (2017). Geometry helps to compare persistence diagrams. ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics, 22.

q_analysis() and simplicial_degree(): connectivity by overlap

The analytic question

In a graph, two nodes are connected or they are not. In a simplicial complex there are degrees of connection: two groups might share one member, or three, or six. Q-analysis (Atkin 1974) takes that seriously.

Two simplices are q-connected when they share at least q + 1 vertices, possibly through a chain of intermediates. Sweep q from high to low and you get a nested picture: at high q only heavily-overlapping groups are linked, and the structure fragments; as q falls, the fragments merge.

Where the merging happens tells you how the system is organised — something neither a degree distribution nor a Betti number reports.

library(honets)
set.seed(1)
m <- matrix(runif(100), 10, 10)
m <- (m + t(m)) / 2
diag(m) <- 0
dimnames(m) <- list(LETTERS[1:10], LETTERS[1:10])
sc <- build_simplicial(m, type = "clique", threshold = 0.5)

Running it

qa <- q_analysis(sc)
qa
Q-Analysis (max q = 3)
  Components: q3:11 q2:10 q1:2 q0:1
  Fragments at q = 3 (11 components)
  Structure: A:3 C:3 D:3 E:3 I:3 B:2 F:2 G:2 H:2 J:2

The q-vector

as.data.frame(qa)
  q components
1 3         11
2 2         10
3 1          2
4 0          1

Read it from the top down. At q = 3 — groups sharing four or more members — the complex is in 11 separate pieces. At q = 2 it is still 10. At q = 1 it drops to 2, and at q = 0 everything is a single component.

The collapse happens between q = 2 and q = 1: this structure is held together by pairwise overlap, not by deep shared membership. Groups here touch each other lightly and rarely share three or more members. A system organised around tightly-interlocking teams would show the opposite profile — few components even at high q.

Seeing the q-vector

plot(qa)

Per-node structure

as.data.frame(qa, what = "nodes")
   node max_q
1     A     3
2     B     2
3     C     3
4     D     3
5     E     3
6     F     2
7     G     2
8     H     2
9     I     3
10    J     2

max_q is the highest level at which each node still participates in a connected group. Nodes A, C, D, E and I reach q = 3; the rest stop at 2. Those five sit inside the most heavily-overlapping part of the complex.

Simplicial degree

simplicial_degree() is the higher-order analogue of node degree: not “how many neighbours” but “how many groups of each size am I in?”

simplicial_degree(sc)
   node d0 d1 d2 d3 total
5     E  1  6  7  2    15
1     A  1  6  6  2    14
9     I  1  5  6  2    13
4     D  1  5  6  1    12
7     G  1  5  4  0     9
10    J  1  5  4  0     9
2     B  1  5  3  0     8
8     H  1  4  4  0     8
3     C  1  3  3  1     7
6     F  1  4  2  0     6

d0 is always 1 — every node is its own vertex. d1 is ordinary graph degree. d2 and d3 are where the higher-order information lives: E is in 7 triangles and 2 tetrahedra, F in only 2 triangles and no tetrahedra, though their graph degrees (6 and 4) are not nearly so far apart.

The table is sorted by total, so the ranking is immediate.

Ordinary degree does not predict it

d <- simplicial_degree(sc)
data.frame(
  measure = c("d1 (graph degree) vs total", "d2 (triangles) vs total"),
  spearman = c(round(cor(d$d1, d$total, method = "spearman"), 3),
               round(cor(d$d2, d$total, method = "spearman"), 3))
)
                     measure spearman
1 d1 (graph degree) vs total    0.894
2    d2 (triangles) vs total    0.963

Graph degree correlates with higher-order degree, but imperfectly — the ranking by total is not the ranking by d1. A node can have many neighbours who are not connected to each other, which produces edges without triangles.

Normalising

simplicial_degree(sc, normalized = TRUE, top = 4)
  node d0        d1        d2         d3     total
1    E  1 0.6666667 0.1944444 0.02380952 0.8849206
2    A  1 0.6666667 0.1666667 0.02380952 0.8571429
3    I  1 0.5555556 0.1666667 0.02380952 0.7460317
4    D  1 0.5555556 0.1666667 0.01190476 0.7341270

normalized = TRUE divides each count by the maximum possible at that dimension, so values are comparable across dimensions and across complexes of different sizes. Use it when comparing datasets; use the raw counts when describing one.

On real data

seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
hon_3 <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 3, min_freq = 5)
sc_hon <- build_simplicial(hon_3, type = "pathway")
q_hon <- q_analysis(sc_hon)
as.data.frame(q_hon)
  q components
1 3         52
2 2         20
3 1          1
4 0          1
simplicial_degree(sc_hon)
       node d0 d1 d2 d3 total
8   Specify  1  8 28 32    68
1   Command  1  8 28 19    55
7   Request  1  8 26 15    49
2   Correct  1  8 26 12    46
3 Frustrate  1  8 26 12    46
4   Inquire  1  8 25 13    46
6    Refine  1  8 27 11    46
5 Interrupt  1  8 26 10    44
9    Verify  1  8 25  8    41

The pathway complex of the coding sessions behaves very differently from the random network above: it stays in many components down to q = 2 and only consolidates at q = 1. And in the degree table, d0 and d1 are identical for every action — a consequence of the saturated first-order structure, where every pair of actions co-occurs. All the discrimination is in d2 and d3, where Specify (32 tetrahedra) separates sharply from Verify (8).

When d1 is constant, ordinary degree centrality is uninformative by construction, and the higher-order degree is the only thing distinguishing the nodes.

What to do next

  • betti_numbers() — holes rather than overlap; the other topological summary of the same complex.
  • build_simplicial() — how the complex is built, and how sensitive it is to threshold.
  • hypergraph_measures() — overlap statistics without the subset-closure assumption.

References

  • Atkin, R. H. (1974). Mathematical Structure in Human Affairs. Heinemann.
  • Johnson, J. (2013). Hypernetworks in the Science of Complex Systems. Imperial College Press.
  • Estrada, E., & Ross, G. J. (2018). Centralities in simplicial complexes. Journal of Theoretical Biology, 438, 46-60.
